taires;  Ital.  ntiliUtristi.  Upholders  of  the

^  Utility  (in  aesthetics):  Ger.  XiitdiMeit; 
Fr.  utilite;  Ital.  utilita.  Value  belonging 
to  an  object  because  it  subserves  some  ex 
ternal  end,  as  opposed  to  intrinsic  or  imme 
diate  value. 

As  an  aesthetic  principle  it  is  used  to 
explain  aesthetic  value  (beauty)  by  showing 
that  the  beautiful  object  serves  some  desirable 
end  (as  a  column  to  support  a  burden),  and 
that  its  aesthetic  value  is  due  to  this,  wholly 
or  in  part.  It  has  been  admitted  as  aesthetic 
principle  chiefly  in  architecture  and  the  lesser 
arts — the  '  dependent  arts.' 

Utility  has  been  recognized  as  contributing 
to  aesthetic  value  by  Socrates,  Plato,  Home, 
Fechncr,  Guyau,  and  in  special  relation  to 
natural  selection  in  forming  types  by  Ilart- 
mann  and  Santayana,  It  was  rejected  by 
Kant.  See  FITNESS  (in  aesthetics).

VACHEROT  —  VACUUM 


Vacherot,  Etienne.  (1809-97.)  Born 
at  Longres,  France,  he  studied  at  Paris  and 
became  professor  of  philosophy  at  the  Sor- 
bonne  in  1839.  Attacked  by  the  clerical 
party  for  his  views,  he  was  for  political  rea 
sons  deprived  of  his  office  in  1852,  and  im 
prisoned  for  tliree  months  in  1859.  In  1871 
he  was  elected  member  of  the  National  As 
sembly  for  the  Department  of  the  Seine. 

Vacuum  [Lat.  vacuus,  empty]  :  Ger.  (das) 
Leere ;  Fr.  (le)  vide  ;  Ital.  (it)  vacuo,  (?7)  vuoto. 
The  condition  of  empty  space  ;  space  unfilled 
by  matter.  Cf.  PLENUM,  and  SPACE. 

The  concepts  of  the  full  (plenum)  and  the 
empty  (vacuum  or  void)  originated  very  early 
in  the  cosmology  of  Pre-Socratic  Philosophy.
